deep.reconstruction:
Context from the previous page: Gauss expands the finite product T = (1+t)(1+at)...(1+a^{n-1}t) = sum_{k=0}^n [n,k]_a a^{k(k-1)/2} t^k. This is the finite q-binomial theorem, which he calls the 'first theorem'. He then puts y = a^{(n-1)/2} t. The k-th and (n-k)-th terms are related by term_{n-k} = term_k * y^{n-2k}, since (n-k)(n-k-1)/2 - k(k-1)/2 = (n-2k)(n-1)/2. Pairing them gives term_k (1 + y^{n-2k}).

This page, n even, n = 2m (finishing the case begun on p.86r):
(i) With a = x^2, the middle term is A = [2m,m]_{x^2} x^{m(m-1)} t^m. Since t = y x^{-(n-1)}, the x-exponent is m(m-1) - m(2m-1) = -m^2. So A = prod_{i=1}^m (1-x^{n+2i})/(1-x^{2i}) * y^{n/2}/x^{n^2/4}, as written.
(ii) The general term with k = m+j becomes [n,m+j]_{x^2} x^{j^2-m^2} y^{m+j}. My check: k^2 - k - (n-1)k = k^2 - 2mk = (k-m)^2 - m^2.
(iii) Dividing by A gives [2m,m+j]/[2m,m] = prod_{i=1}^{j} (1-x^{n-2i+2})/(1-x^{n+2i}).
(iv) On the product side, the first half of the factors gives y^m x^{-m^2} prod_{i=1}^m (1+x^{2i-1}/y). The second half gives prod_{i=1}^m (1+x^{2i-1}y). The prefactor y^m x^{-m^2} divided by A equals 1/[2m,m].

Result, which Gauss calls the 2nd theorem (n even):
1 + sum_{j=1}^{n/2} prod_{i=1}^j (1-x^{n-2i+2})/(1-x^{n+2i}) * x^{j^2}(y^j + y^{-j}) = prod_{i=1}^{n/2} (1+x^{2i-1}y)(1+x^{2i-1}/y) * prod_{i=1}^{n/2} (1-x^{2i})/(1-x^{n+2i}).

Section 3, n odd, n = 2m+1:
(i) The pairing now leaves no middle term. The last pair is k = m: [n,m]_a a^{(n-1)(n-3)/8} t^{(n-1)/2} (1+y).
(ii) The pair before it has numerator ending in 1-a^{(n+5)/2}, denominator ending in 1-a^{(n-3)/2}, and factor a^{(n-3)(n-5)/8} t^{(n-3)/2}(1+y^3). All of this is correct.
(iii) With a = x^2, the last pair equals [n,m]_{x^2} y^m x^{-m(m+1)} (1+y). Gauss writes it as B x^{1/4}(y^{1/2}+y^{-1/2}). Hence B = [n,m]_{x^2} y^{n/2} x^{-n^2/4}, because (m+1/2)^2 = n^2/4; this is confirmed on the next page.
(iv) Dividing by B, the series becomes sum_{j=0}^m c_j x^{(j+1/2)^2} (y^{j+1/2} + y^{-j-1/2}). Here c_j = [n,m-j]/[n,m] = prod_{i=1}^j (1-x^{n+1-2i})/(1-x^{n+1+2i}). This gives the coefficients (1-x^{n-1})/(1-x^{n+3}), then also (1-x^{n-3})/(1-x^{n+5}), and the exponents 1/4, 9/4, 25/4. There are (n+1)/2 terms.
(v) The product is T = prod_{l=-m}^{m} (1+x^{2l}y). Its first (n-1)/2 factors equal y^{(n-1)/2} x^{-(n^2-1)/4} (1+x^{n-1}/y)...(1+x^2/y).

The next page completes the odd case. The remaining factors are (1+y)(1+x^2 y)...(1+x^{n-1}y), and the result is the 3rd theorem:
sum_{j=0}^m c_j x^{(j+1/2)^2}(y^{j+1/2}+y^{-j-1/2}) = x^{1/4}(y^{1/2}+y^{-1/2}) prod_{i=1}^m (1+x^{2i}y)(1+x^{2i}/y) * prod_{i=1}^m (1-x^{2i})/(1-x^{n+1+2i}).

Purpose: these are finite (polynomial) forms of the Jacobi triple product. Letting n -> infinity on the next page gives sum x^{k^2} y^k = prod (1+x^{2i-1}y)(1+x^{2i-1}/y)(1-x^{2i}) and its 'odd' companion. Overall this is a derivation of the triple product identity from the finite q-binomial (Rothe–Gauss) theorem via Gaussian polynomials.
errors: First term of the odd-case series is written x^{1/4}(y+y^{-1/2}); it should be x^{1/4}(y^{1/2}+y^{-1/2}). This is a slip, written correctly on the next page.
In the denominator of the penultimate odd-case term, the last factor should be 1-a^{(n-3)/2} = 1-a^{m-1}. The writing looks like 1-a^{n/2-3}, which would be a slip if read literally.
In the even-case product, the factor 1-x^4 was overwritten or struck; the intended value is 1-x^4. No mathematical error.
Otherwise all exponents, coefficient ratios and term counts check out.

results.what: Finite even-n identity: sum_{j=-m}^{m} ([2m,m+j]/[2m,m])_{x^2} x^{j^2} y^j = prod_{i=1}^m (1+x^{2i-1}y)(1+x^{2i-1}/y) / [2m,m]_{x^2}, obtained by symmetric pairing of the q-binomial expansion
results.modern_name: Finite (polynomial) form of the Jacobi triple product, i.e. the q-binomial theorem in symmetric form
results.usually_credited_to: Cauchy (1843) and later MacMahon / Sylvester; triple product to Jacobi (1829)

results.what: Finite odd-n companion with half-integer powers: sum_j c_j x^{(j+1/2)^2}(y^{j+1/2}+y^{-j-1/2}) = x^{1/4}(y^{1/2}+y^{-1/2}) prod (1+x^{2i}y)(1+x^{2i}/y) / [n,(n-1)/2]
Derivation of the triple product (next page) by letting n -> infinity
results.usually_credited_to: Jacobi 1829 (Gauss's priority from the Nachlass, published in Werke III, is acknowledged)

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's possession of the triple product and his work with Gaussian polynomials and Rothe's q-binomial theorem are documented from the Nachlass (Werke III). This page is a careful finite-to-infinite derivation, which is a notable unpublished detail anticipating Cauchy's 1843 method, but it is consistent with what historians already attribute to him.
